passages.text: A public library is a place where anyone can read and borrow books for free. Most libraries also have newspapers, computers, and quiet rooms for studying. To borrow books, you need a library card, which is usually free for people who live in the city. You can take a book home and keep it for a few weeks. If you return it late, you may have to pay a small fine. Many libraries also have special story hours for children, where a librarian reads books aloud. Today, some libraries even lend e-books that you can read on your phone without visiting the building at all.

The relationship between social media use and mental health has attracted considerable attention from researchers in recent years. Several studies have found associations between heavy social media use and increased rates of anxiety and depression, particularly among adolescents. One proposed mechanism is social comparison: when users are exposed to idealized images and curated accounts of others' lives, they may develop negative self-perceptions. However, researchers caution against overly simplistic conclusions. Some studies suggest that the quality of online interactions, rather than the quantity of time spent, is the more significant variable. Passive scrolling has been linked to worse outcomes than active engagement with communities of interest. The picture is further complicated by the fact that individuals with pre-existing mental health difficulties may be more drawn to heavy social media use, making it difficult to determine the direction of causality.

Cognitive biases are systematic patterns of deviation from rational judgment that affect human decision-making. Unlike random errors, biases are predictable and consistent, arising from the mental shortcuts — known as heuristics — that the brain uses to process information efficiently. The confirmation bias, for instance, leads individuals to seek and weight evidence that confirms their pre-existing beliefs while discounting contradictory information. The availability heuristic causes people to overestimate the likelihood of events that are easily recalled, such as plane crashes, while underestimating more statistically common risks. Research by psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky demonstrated that these biases are not limited to uninformed or irrational individuals; they affect experts and novices alike. Understanding cognitive biases has practical implications in fields ranging from public policy to medical diagnosis, where unrecognized biases can lead to systematic errors with significant consequences.

The concept of epistemic injustice, introduced by philosopher Miranda Fricker, describes forms of harm done to individuals specifically in their capacity as knowers — that is, as agents who hold and communicate knowledge. Fricker identifies two primary forms: testimonial injustice, which occurs when a speaker receives a credibility deficit due to identity prejudice, and hermeneutical injustice, which arises when gaps in collective interpretive resources place someone at a disadvantage in understanding or articulating their own social experience. A paradigm case of the latter is the historical absence of the concept of sexual harassment, which left those who experienced it without the shared vocabulary necessary to render their experience intelligible to others or to themselves. Critics have extended and complicated Fricker's original framework, noting that epistemic injustice can also be perpetrated by institutions and structural conditions, not only by individual agents engaging in prejudicial credibility assessments.

Sleep is very important for good health. When we sleep, our bodies rest and repair themselves. Most adults need between seven and nine hours of sleep each night. Children and teenagers need even more sleep than adults. Without enough sleep, people feel tired and find it hard to concentrate. They may also get sick more easily because sleep helps the body fight illness. Scientists say that sleeping at the same time every night is helpful. Turning off screens before bed can also make it easier to fall asleep. Good sleep habits can improve mood, memory, and overall health.

Libraries are very useful places for communities. They offer books, magazines, and other resources that people can borrow for free. Many libraries also provide computers and internet access for those who do not have them at home. Children can join reading programs to improve their reading skills. Libraries are often quiet places where students can study. They also organize events such as book clubs and storytelling sessions. A library card is usually free to obtain. Librarians are trained to help people find information they need. Libraries are important because they make knowledge available to everyone, not just those who can afford to buy books.

Street markets exist in almost every country in the world. People come to them not only to buy fruit, vegetables, clothes, and other goods, but also to meet friends and enjoy the lively atmosphere. Prices in street markets are often lower than in regular shops, partly because sellers do not pay rent for a large building. Bargaining is common: buyers and sellers discuss the price until they agree. In recent years, however, many street markets have become smaller or have closed. Supermarkets and online shopping offer more comfort, and many young people prefer them. Still, in many cities the old markets survive, loved for their special character that no website can copy.

People have enjoyed frozen desserts for a very long time. More than two thousand years ago, rich Romans sent runners to the mountains to bring back snow, which they mixed with honey and fruit. Ice cream as we know it, made with milk and sugar, probably developed in Italy and France a few hundred years ago. At first it was a luxury that only kings and wealthy families could afford, because ice was rare and expensive. Everything changed in the nineteenth century, when new machines made it possible to produce ice cheaply. Ice cream quickly became a treat for everyone, sold in streets and shops around the world. Today, people eat billions of liters of ice cream every year.

In the past two decades, social media platforms such as Instagram, Twitter, and TikTok have transformed the way people communicate and share information. While these platforms offer significant benefits, including the ability to connect with friends and family across the world, researchers have raised concerns about their effects on mental health. Studies suggest that excessive use of social media is associated with increased rates of anxiety, depression, and loneliness, particularly among teenagers. One reason for this may be the phenomenon of social comparison, in which users compare their lives to the carefully curated images of others. Additionally, the algorithms that power social media platforms are designed to maximize engagement, often by promoting content that triggers strong emotional reactions. Despite growing awareness of these risks, social media use continues to rise globally, and many people feel unable to disconnect from their devices.

Coffee is one of the most popular drinks in the world. Many people drink it in the morning to help them feel more awake. Coffee contains caffeine, a natural substance that stimulates the brain and reduces feelings of tiredness. Research has shown that moderate coffee consumption — about two to three cups per day — may have health benefits, including improved concentration and a lower risk of certain diseases. However, drinking too much coffee can cause side effects such as anxiety, difficulty sleeping, and an increased heart rate. Experts recommend that people pay attention to how their bodies respond to caffeine and adjust their intake accordingly. Pregnant women and people with certain health conditions are often advised to limit or avoid coffee.

Urban parks play an important role in city life. They provide residents with open green spaces where they can exercise, relax, and socialize. Research has shown that access to parks is associated with lower levels of stress and improved mental health. Parks also serve environmental functions: trees and plants help clean the air and reduce city temperatures, easing what is known as the urban heat island effect — the tendency of cities to be warmer than their surroundings. In many cities, parks serve as gathering places for cultural events, markets, and community activities. However, the distribution of parks across urban areas is not always equal. Lower-income neighborhoods often have fewer or lower-quality parks than wealthier areas, raising concerns about environmental justice. City planners are increasingly recognizing the importance of equitable green space distribution as part of sustainable urban development.

Urban noise is increasingly recognized as more than a mere nuisance. Prolonged exposure to traffic noise has been linked to elevated blood pressure, disturbed sleep, and impaired concentration in schoolchildren. Unlike air pollution, however, noise leaves no visible trace, which may explain why it has historically received far less regulatory attention. Some European cities have begun to treat noise as a genuine public health issue: they have introduced quiet zones, lowered speed limits at night, and required developers to install sound insulation in new buildings. Skeptics argue that such measures impose significant costs on businesses and drivers while producing benefits that are difficult to measure. Health researchers respond that the costs of inaction, though less visible, are ultimately borne by hospitals and schools, and that measuring a problem poorly is not a reason to ignore it.

Everyone knows that sleep is important, but many people do not get enough of it. Scientists say that most adults need seven to nine hours of sleep every night. During sleep, the brain stays busy: it stores new memories and cleans out waste materials that build up during the day. This is why students who sleep well after studying usually remember the material better than students who stay up all night. A lack of sleep does more than make you tired. It makes it harder to concentrate, slows your reactions, and can even weaken the body's ability to fight illness. Experts suggest simple habits for better sleep: go to bed at the same time every night, avoid coffee in the evening, and keep phones out of the bedroom.

Common sense suggests that a person in trouble is safer in a crowd, since more people are available to help. Research in social psychology points to the opposite conclusion. In a series of classic experiments, participants who believed they were the only witness to an emergency usually acted quickly, while those who thought others were also watching often did nothing. Psychologists call this the bystander effect, and they explain it through a process known as diffusion of responsibility: when many witnesses are present, each individual feels less personally obligated to act, assuming that someone else will step in. Awareness of the effect appears to weaken it. People who have learned about the bystander effect are more likely to intervene, and safety courses now teach a practical remedy: instead of appealing to a crowd in general, point at one specific person and ask that person directly for help.

The World Health Organization (WHO) recently conducted a worldwide study on mental health problems. The main purpose of the study was to find out whether mental illnesses and their symptoms are the same all over the world. Researchers also investigated whether certain psychological disorders are more common in some countries than in others.

Many anthropologists claim that people in different cultures suffer from different psychological symptoms and disorders. The results of WHO's study, however, showed that people around the world have similar mental health problems, although people in different countries may give different names to the same set of symptoms. For example, what is called "anxiety" in the United States may be called "kidney weakness" in China and "fatigue" in Europe.

WHO's researchers studied more than 25,000 patients in 14 countries. They found that 24% of these patients were suffering from well-defined psychological disorders, the most common ones being depression and nervous fatigue. The study showed that people all over the world suffer from these disorders. However, some illnesses appear to be more common in certain countries than in others. For instance, the percentage of people suffering from depression was found to be highest in Chile and Brazil, and lowest in China, Japan and Nigeria.

The Great Pyramid of Giza, built around 2560 BCE, is the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World and the only one still largely intact. It was constructed as a tomb for the Egyptian Pharaoh Khufu and remained the tallest man-made structure in the world for over 3,800 years. The pyramid required an estimated 2.3 million stone blocks, each weighing between 2.5 and 15 tons. For centuries, historians debated how the ancient Egyptians built such a massive monument without modern tools. While some proposed extraordinary explanations, most scholars now believe the pyramids were built by an organized workforce of paid laborers, not by slaves as was once commonly thought. Recent archaeological discoveries, including workers' villages and administrative records, support this view. The Sphinx, a limestone statue with the body of a lion and the head of a human, stands nearby and is believed to have been built during the reign of Pharaoh Khafre, who succeeded Khufu.

Highway travel is the lifeblood of modern industrial nations. But in the United States, as in many other countries, major thoroughfares are perpetually overcrowded. During peak travel hours in big American cities, dense highway traffic slows to less than 56 kilometers per hour. In London, cars and buses move at an average speed of 20 kilometers per hour – no faster than the horse-drawn carriages of a hundred years ago.

Then why not simply build more roads? The main reason is that highway construction – whether building new roads or expanding old ones – is enormously expensive, particularly in urban areas. For instance, it cost more than 8 billion dollars to reconstruct an 11-kilometer stretch of the Central Artery in Boston. So, if existing highways are to accommodate expanding urban areas, people must somehow learn to use these roadways more efficiently.

One possible way is to develop an automated highway system: a lane or set of lanes where specially equipped cars, trucks and buses would "drive themselves" under computer control. Networks of small computers installed in vehicles and in the roadways could coordinate the flow of traffic, increasing efficiency and safety.

On automated highways, vehicles could travel closely together and merge smoothly, without the usual uncertainties and potential for collisions. As a result, a typical highway lane that now carries 2,000 vehicles per hour could handle 6,000 with no reduction in speed. Surprisingly, turning conventional roadways into high-tech highways would be less expensive than building more roads or widening existing ones.

The coffee plant is native to Ethiopia, where, according to legend, it was discovered by a goat herder named Kaldi in the ninth century. Kaldi noticed that his goats became unusually energetic after eating berries from a certain tree. He brought the berries to a monastery, where the monks made a drink from them and found that it kept them awake during their long evening prayers.

From Ethiopia, coffee spread to the Arabian Peninsula, where it was first cultivated in Yemen in the fifteenth century. By the sixteenth century, coffeehouses known as "qahveh khaneh" had become popular social gathering places throughout the Middle East. People came to these establishments to drink coffee, listen to music, play chess, and discuss the latest news.

Coffee was introduced to Europe by Ottoman Turks in the seventeenth century. Although the drink was initially met with suspicion — Pope Clement VIII was asked to ban it as "the drink of the devil" before he tasted it and reportedly gave his approval — coffeehouses soon became as popular in Europe as they were in the Middle East. These establishments played an important role in intellectual life, becoming centers of discussion and the birthplace of many business ventures.

In ancient Greece, doctors were people of great importance. Although some had permanent clinics in towns, most doctors travelled from place to place to see their patients. They placed great emphasis on cleanliness, never touching a wound and examining it only with the aid of instruments. They questioned patients closely about their symptoms and looked for factors in people's lives and surroundings that might affect their health. Greek doctors also prepared herbal and mineral mixtures with antiseptic properties for the treatment of wounds. Although not always beneficial to patients, the procedures they employed involved much care and caution.

In addition to addressing the physical aspects of disease, Greek doctors did not neglect the spiritual side of healing. When their own efforts failed, they recommended that their patients visit one of the many "asclepieia" – temples dedicated to the patron god of physicians, Asclepius, and his daughters, Hygeia (health) and Panacea (healing). At the temples, patients relaxed in beautiful surroundings and read inscriptions on marble pillars that told of miraculous remedies provided by the gods. It was believed that if they spent the night in the sacred hall, Asclepius would appear to them as they slept and give them a "dream drug" or even perform "dream surgery," and cure them.

The greatest of all doctors in ancient Greece was Hippocrates. A physician and surgeon, he headed a medical school on the Aegean island of Kos. His work and that of his followers is contained in the Corpus Hippocraticum, over 70 volumes that range in content from detailed case histories to thoughts on the practice of medicine, the effects of the environment on health and, most importantly, prognosis. It was the Hippocratic school's concentration on the latter that distinguished it from other medical schools of thought that were active at the time. While non-Hippocratic doctors only tried to identify symptoms and make diagnoses, the Kos physicians went one step further and tried to predict a patient's prospects of recovery.

Since the early 19th century, a tall, wooden clock has stood in the lobby of the George Hotel in North Yorkshire, England. The clock kept perfect time until the day the owner of the hotel died. Then it stopped and nobody could fix it. The new owner of the George decided to leave it standing in its place and enjoyed telling the story to his guests.

In 1875, an American songwriter named Henry Work came to stay at the George. He asked about the big clock and was told the story of how it had stopped working. Work was inspired to write a song about the clock. He called it "My Grandfather's Clock," and it became extremely popular. Because of this song, tall clocks that stand on the floor came to be known as grandfather clocks.

Marie Curie is one of the most celebrated scientists in history. Born in Warsaw, Poland in 1867, she showed exceptional academic ability from an early age but was unable to study at university in Poland, where higher education was closed to women. In 1891, she moved to Paris, where she enrolled at the Sorbonne University and earned degrees in both physics and mathematics.

Together with her husband Pierre Curie, Marie conducted groundbreaking research on radioactivity — a term she herself coined. In 1898, the couple discovered two new chemical elements, polonium (named after Marie's homeland) and radium. In 1903, Marie and Pierre shared the Nobel Prize in Physics for their research. When Pierre died in a road accident in 1906, Marie took over his position as Professor of Physics at the Sorbonne, becoming the first woman to hold a professorship at the institution.

In 1911, Marie Curie received a second Nobel Prize, this time in Chemistry, becoming the only person to have won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. Her work had far-reaching consequences for medicine: the use of X-rays in hospitals expanded enormously because of research she conducted during World War I. Despite these achievements, Curie faced significant gender discrimination throughout her career, being refused entry to many scientific societies solely because she was a woman.

The Renaissance was a cultural and intellectual movement that began in Italy in the fourteenth century and gradually spread across Europe over the following two centuries. The word "renaissance" means "rebirth" in French, reflecting the period's revival of interest in the art, literature, and philosophy of ancient Greece and Rome. Renaissance thinkers, known as humanists, emphasized the potential of the individual and the importance of education, reason, and civic virtue. The arts flourished during this period, producing extraordinary works by figures such as Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, and Raphael. These artists broke from the rigid conventions of medieval art, using techniques such as perspective and chiaroscuro to create more realistic and emotionally expressive works. The Renaissance also saw significant advances in science and exploration. Figures like Galileo Galilei challenged established religious and scientific doctrine, and European explorers like Christopher Columbus opened up new trade routes and expanded European knowledge of the world. The printing press, invented by Johannes Gutenberg around 1440, played a crucial role in spreading Renaissance ideas by making books more widely available.

Edith Cavell is the name of a mountain in Canada, streets in England, Belgium and Mauritius, and hospitals and schools throughout the world. In St. Martin's Place, just off London's Trafalgar Square, a statue of Edith Cavell prominently displays her words: "Patriotism is not enough. I must have no hatred or bitterness for anyone." But who was this woman and why has she been honored so widely?

Edith Cavell was a British nurse. She worked in various London hospitals for some years before moving to Brussels, Belgium, to become the head of nursing at the Berkendael Institute, a training school for nurses. She proved to be both a talented teacher and a capable administrator, transforming the institute from a small clinic into a teaching hospital with an international reputation.

In 1914, World War I broke out and the Germans occupied Belgium. Although Cavell was a British citizen and could have returned home to safety, she refused to leave Brussels. Now the hospital was filled with wounded German soldiers. However, Cavell cared for all her patients with devotion, regardless of their nationality.

One day a Belgian man arrived at Berkendael with two British soldiers who had been separated from their units. He explained that, if found by the Germans, the soldiers faced certain death. Would Cavell hide them? She agreed, even though she knew that she was putting herself in danger. Gradually, more and more British, French and Belgian soldiers, some of them seriously wounded, found their way to Berkendael. Cavell took care of them, gave them false identification papers and helped them escape to Holland, which was a neutral country. By 1915, she had lodged more than two hundred soldiers and helped them to escape. But the Germans grew suspicious. Eventually they arrested her and tried her for collaborating with the enemy. Cavell made a full confession and was sentenced to death. Despite international appeals for clemency, Cavell was executed by firing squad on October 12, 1915.

The Amazon rainforest covers approximately 5.5 million square kilometers across nine South American countries, with about 60% located in Brazil. It is the world's largest tropical rainforest and is home to an estimated 10% of all species on earth. Scientists estimate that a single hectare of Amazon forest may contain over 400 distinct tree species — more biodiversity than can be found in the entire continent of Europe.

The Amazon basin contains the world's largest river system. The Amazon River discharges more water into the ocean than any other river on earth — roughly 20% of all freshwater that flows into the world's oceans. During the rainy season, the river can extend up to 50 kilometers in width, flooding vast areas of surrounding forest.

Despite its importance, the Amazon rainforest is under severe threat. Each year, millions of acres of forest are cleared through logging and burning to make room for agriculture and cattle ranching. Scientists warn that if deforestation continues at its current rate, the rainforest could reach a 'tipping point' beyond which it would be unable to sustain itself and would begin to transform into a dry savanna. The consequences for global climate would be catastrophic, since the forest absorbs enormous quantities of carbon dioxide and produces vast amounts of oxygen.

Dogs are popular pets around the world. They are known for being friendly and loyal to their owners. People keep dogs for many reasons. Some people want a companion at home, while others use dogs to help them with tasks such as guarding the house. Dogs need food, water, and exercise every day. They also need to visit a veterinarian regularly to stay healthy. Most dogs enjoy playing and spending time with their families. Taking care of a dog is a big responsibility, but many people find it very rewarding.

Urbanization is one of the most significant global trends of the twenty-first century. As more people move from rural areas to cities in search of employment and better living conditions, urban populations are growing at an unprecedented rate. By 2050, it is estimated that nearly seventy percent of the world population will live in urban areas. This rapid growth presents both opportunities and challenges. On the positive side, cities tend to offer better access to education, healthcare, and economic opportunities. However, the strain placed on infrastructure, housing, and public services can be enormous. Traffic congestion, pollution, and social inequality are among the most pressing problems facing rapidly growing cities today. Effective urban planning is therefore essential to ensure that cities remain livable and sustainable for all residents.

The placebo effect refers to the measurable, real improvement in a patient's condition that results not from an active medical treatment but from the patient's belief that they are receiving one. Documented extensively in clinical research, the phenomenon challenges simplistic assumptions about the relationship between mind and body. Studies have shown that even when patients are informed that they are receiving a placebo, a significant therapeutic effect can still be observed — a phenomenon known as the "open-label placebo." This suggests that the brain's anticipatory mechanisms can trigger genuine physiological responses, including the release of endorphins and changes in neurological activity. Critics have raised ethical concerns about the use of placebos in medical practice, arguing that deception undermines the principle of informed consent. Proponents, however, contend that understanding and harnessing the placebo effect ethically represents a frontier for medicine that remains largely unexplored. The debate reflects broader tensions between evidence-based medicine and the recognition that subjective experience plays a fundamental role in health outcomes.

Climate change poses a significant threat to global food production. Rising temperatures, shifting rainfall patterns, and more frequent extreme weather events are altering the conditions under which crops grow. Warmer temperatures can accelerate crop growth cycles, but they can also reduce yields by increasing heat stress on plants and disrupting pollination. Changes in precipitation threaten to cause both droughts in traditionally fertile regions and flooding in others. Scientists estimate that without adaptation measures, yields of staple crops such as wheat, rice, and maize could decline substantially in many parts of the world by the end of the century. In response, agricultural researchers are developing heat-resistant and drought-tolerant crop varieties, and farmers are experimenting with altered planting schedules and irrigation methods. While these adaptations can reduce some of the damage, experts warn that they cannot fully offset the impacts of continued warming, making emissions reduction a necessary complement to agricultural adjustment.

The gig economy — characterized by short-term contracts, freelance work, and on-demand labor platforms — has grown substantially in the past decade, driven by digital technology and shifting labor market dynamics. Proponents argue that gig work offers flexibility and autonomy that traditional employment cannot match, allowing workers to set their own hours and choose their assignments. Critics, however, contend that this flexibility comes at a significant cost. Gig workers are typically classified as independent contractors rather than employees, which means they are often ineligible for benefits such as health insurance, paid leave, and retirement contributions. They also lack employment protections such as minimum wage guarantees and the right to collective bargaining. Research suggests that while some gig workers — particularly skilled professionals who use platforms by choice — benefit from the arrangement, a significant proportion are low-income workers who rely on platform work as a primary source of income and face considerable economic insecurity. The regulatory response has been inconsistent across jurisdictions.

The formation of scientific consensus is a social as well as an epistemic process, shaped not only by the accumulation of evidence but also by the institutional structures, funding dynamics, and professional incentives that govern scientific practice. Historian of science Naomi Oreskes has argued that consensus is the most reliable indicator of scientific knowledge available, more so than any single study, because it represents the collective judgment of a community of experts over time. Critics have raised two distinct objections. The first is sociological: consensus can be artificially manufactured by powerful institutional interests, as illustrated by documented efforts of the tobacco and fossil fuel industries to generate the appearance of scientific uncertainty where expert agreement existed. The second is epistemological: consensus, like any collective belief, is susceptible to entrenched error, and paradigm shifts often originate in the rejection of prevailing consensus by heterodox thinkers. Neither objection, its proponents would insist, constitutes grounds for dismissing scientific consensus as a reliable epistemic resource; rather, they illuminate the conditions under which consensus should be treated with heightened scrutiny.

Exercise is one of the best things you can do for your body and mind. Regular physical activity helps keep your heart healthy and your muscles strong. It can also help you maintain a healthy weight. Exercise does not have to be difficult or expensive. Simple activities like walking, cycling, or swimming are very effective. Doctors recommend that adults get at least thirty minutes of moderate exercise most days of the week. Children need even more — at least one hour per day. Exercise can also improve your mood and reduce feelings of stress and anxiety. Even small amounts of physical activity are better than none at all.

Recycling is the process of converting waste materials into new products, reducing the need for raw materials and decreasing the amount of waste sent to landfills. Common recyclable materials include paper, glass, plastic, and metal. Recycling benefits the environment in several ways: it conserves natural resources, reduces energy consumption, and helps lower greenhouse gas emissions. For example, recycling aluminum requires approximately ninety-five percent less energy than producing new aluminum from raw materials. Despite these benefits, recycling rates vary widely across countries and communities. Successful recycling programs depend on clear public education, convenient collection systems, and markets for recycled materials. Critics note that while recycling is valuable, it should be seen as one part of a broader waste reduction strategy that also includes reducing consumption and reusing products.

Artificial intelligence is increasingly being applied in medical settings, with the potential to improve diagnostic accuracy and healthcare efficiency. Machine learning algorithms can analyze medical images — such as X-rays, MRI scans, and pathology slides — with a speed and consistency that may exceed human performance in certain tasks. In dermatology, AI systems have demonstrated diagnostic accuracy for skin conditions comparable to or better than that of board-certified specialists. Despite these promising results, challenges remain. AI systems are only as reliable as the data they are trained on, and biases in training datasets — such as underrepresentation of certain patient populations — can lead to unequal performance across demographic groups. The integration of AI into clinical practice also raises questions about accountability: when an algorithm contributes to a diagnostic error, it is unclear how responsibility should be allocated among algorithm developers, healthcare institutions, and treating physicians.

CRISPR-Cas9, a gene-editing technology developed in the early 2010s, has made it possible to modify DNA sequences with unprecedented precision and affordability. In biomedical research, CRISPR has accelerated efforts to understand genetic diseases and develop potential therapies, with clinical trials underway for conditions such as sickle cell disease. The technology has also generated profound ethical debates. The most contentious application involves heritable genome editing — modifying embryo DNA in ways that would be passed to future generations. Critics argue that heritable editing crosses a fundamental ethical line by making permanent germline changes without the consent of future individuals, and risks introducing unpredictable genetic consequences. Proponents counter that if heritable editing can prevent severe genetic diseases, its potential benefit may justify carefully regulated use. In 2018, a Chinese scientist announced the birth of gene-edited babies, an event widely condemned by the scientific community and which prompted calls for international governance frameworks.

The relationship between language and thought has been one of the most contested questions in cognitive science. The hypothesis associated with Benjamin Lee Whorf — known as the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis or linguistic relativity — holds that the language one speaks shapes, to some degree, how one perceives and conceptualizes reality. In its strong form, linguistic determinism claims that language determines thought, making it impossible to think thoughts for which no linguistic expression exists. This strong version has been largely rejected: cross-linguistic studies show that speakers of different languages can perform the same cognitive operations regardless of whether their language encodes the relevant distinctions. The weak form — linguistic relativity — has, however, retained more scientific credibility. Research by Lera Boroditsky and colleagues has demonstrated that language can influence non-linguistic cognition in domains such as spatial reasoning, time perception, and color discrimination. These findings suggest that while language does not imprison thought, it may subtly orient habitual patterns of attention and categorization without making alternative conceptualizations impossible.

Water is essential for all living things. Our bodies are made of about sixty percent water, and we need to drink enough every day to stay healthy. Without water, a person can survive only a few days. Water helps the body carry nutrients to cells, remove waste, and control temperature. Drinking at least eight glasses of water a day is often recommended, though the exact amount depends on body size, activity level, and the weather. In addition to drinking, water is used for cooking, cleaning, and growing food. In some parts of the world, clean water is hard to find. Saving and protecting water is important for everyone.

Learning a second language has many benefits beyond being able to communicate with more people. Research has shown that bilingual individuals often develop stronger cognitive skills, including better attention, multitasking ability, and problem-solving. Speaking two or more languages may also delay the onset of age-related cognitive decline, including symptoms of dementia. Children who grow up in bilingual households tend to acquire both languages naturally and simultaneously. Adults can also learn new languages effectively, though the process often requires more deliberate effort. Immersion — surrounding oneself with the language through conversation, media, and travel — is considered one of the most effective methods for adults. Despite the challenges, learning a second language is considered a valuable investment in both professional and personal development, and can also promote cultural understanding and empathy across communities.

Ocean pollution is a growing environmental crisis with serious consequences for marine ecosystems and human health. Among the most significant contributors is plastic waste, which enters waterways through rivers, coastal dumping, and stormwater runoff. Once in the ocean, plastic breaks down into microplastics — tiny particles ingested by marine animals that can accumulate up the food chain and eventually reach human consumers. Chemical pollutants, including agricultural runoff containing fertilizers, contribute to hypoxic dead zones — areas so depleted of oxygen that most marine life cannot survive. Noise pollution from shipping traffic and sonar technology disrupts cetaceans such as whales and dolphins, which rely on sound for navigation and communication. Addressing ocean pollution requires regulatory action — such as bans on single-use plastics and controls on agricultural runoff — as well as international cooperation, since ocean currents distribute pollutants across national boundaries.

The rapid growth of cities is one of the defining features of the twenty-first century: the United Nations estimates that by 2050, approximately two-thirds of the global population will live in urban areas. This expansion comes at a significant cost to biodiversity. The conversion of natural habitats to built environments destroys ecosystems many species depend on, contributing to population decline and local extinction. Species richness typically decreases as urbanization intensifies. However, the relationship between cities and biodiversity is not uniformly negative. Urban green spaces — including parks, green roofs, community gardens, and tree-lined streets — can serve as refuges and corridors for certain species, particularly generalists capable of adapting to human-modified environments. Research in urban ecology has shown that well-designed cities can support surprising levels of biodiversity. The challenge for urban planners is to integrate ecological concerns into city design from the outset, rather than treating biodiversity conservation as an afterthought.

The concept of democratic backsliding — the gradual weakening of democratic institutions through formally legal processes — has become a central preoccupation of contemporary political science. Unlike classical coups, modern democratic erosion typically proceeds through incremental steps: manipulation of electoral rules, appointment of partisan loyalists to independent institutions, restriction of press freedom through regulatory pressure, and systematic delegitimization of political opponents. Scholars such as Levitsky and Way challenged the assumption that democracy, once established, tends toward consolidation, demonstrating that many regimes were in fact competitive authoritarian systems — maintaining electoral competition while systematically tilting the playing field toward incumbents. A related concept is populist constitutionalism, whereby elected leaders invoke democratic mandates to dismantle the checks and balances democracy requires. The paradox this generates — the use of democratic procedures to undermine democratic institutions — has proven difficult for legal systems and international actors to address, since the tools of erosion are formally legitimate even when their cumulative effect is the hollowing-out of meaningful democratic participation.

Since the early 19th century, a tall, wooden clock has stood in the lobby of the George Hotel in North Yorkshire, England. The clock kept perfect time until the day the owner of the hotel died. Then it stopped and nobody could fix it. The new owner of the George decided to leave it standing in its place and enjoyed telling the story to his guests. In 1875, an American songwriter named Henry Work came to stay at the George. He asked about the big clock and was told the story of how it had stopped working. Work was inspired to write a song about the clock. He called it "My Grandfather's Clock," and it became extremely popular. Because of this song, tall clocks that stand on the floor came to be known as grandfather clocks.

Camels are famous for living in hot, dry deserts. Many people think that a camel keeps water in its hump, but this is not true. The hump is full of fat, which the camel uses for energy when there is no food. A camel can drink a huge amount of water very quickly — more than 100 liters in about ten minutes — and then walk for days without drinking again. Camels also have long eyelashes that protect their eyes from sand, and wide feet that help them walk on soft ground. For thousands of years, people in the desert have used camels to carry heavy loads across long distances.

The World Health Organization (WHO) recently conducted a worldwide study on mental health problems. The main purpose of the study was to find out whether mental illnesses and their symptoms are the same all over the world. Researchers also investigated whether certain psychological disorders are more common in some countries than in others. Many anthropologists claim that people in different cultures suffer from different psychological symptoms and disorders. The results of WHO's study, however, showed that people around the world have similar mental health problems, although people in different countries may give different names to the same set of symptoms. For example, what is called "anxiety" in the United States may be called "kidney weakness" in China and "fatigue" in Europe. WHO's researchers studied more than 25,000 patients in 14 countries. They found that 24% of these patients were suffering from well-defined psychological disorders, the most common ones being depression and nervous fatigue. The study showed that people all over the world suffer from these disorders. However, some illnesses appear to be more common in certain countries than in others. For instance, the percentage of people suffering from depression was found to be highest in Chile and Brazil, and lowest in China, Japan and Nigeria.

Mark Twain once said that accident is the greatest of all inventors. If you have any doubt about this, go into your kitchen and look around. You might find a Teflon pan, a microwave oven, or a box of matches. Accident played a role in the invention of all these common household items. But not everyone can make the most of an accident. The difference between inventors and the rest of us is that they see possibilities where we see only everyday events. In the words of Louis Pasteur, "Chance favors only the prepared mind." One such mind belonged to a pharmacist named John Walker. One day in 1826, he was using a wooden stick to mix potassium chlorate and antimony sulphide. Unable to clean the mixture off the stick, he tried to scrape it off against the stone floor and was startled to see the stick burst into flames. He realized that he had stumbled upon a compound that could be used to light a fire easily. Walker was marketing the first friction match. Sometimes, when an inventor is seeking a solution to a problem, the answer appears out of nowhere. In 1928, Alexander Fleming was searching for a means of treating bacterial infections. One day some dust drifted through the open window of his laboratory, landing in a petri dish where he was growing a culture of bacteria. It caused parts of the culture to change color. Instead of throwing out the contaminated petri dish, he looked at its contents under the microscope. He realized that the bacteria were being destroyed by mold found in the dust, and from this came penicillin, a medicine that has saved countless lives.

In ancient Greece, doctors were people of great importance. Although some had permanent clinics in towns, most doctors travelled from place to place to see their patients. They placed great emphasis on cleanliness, never touching a wound and examining it only with the aid of instruments. They questioned patients closely about their symptoms and looked for factors in people's lives and surroundings that might affect their health. Greek doctors also prepared herbal and mineral mixtures with antiseptic properties for the treatment of wounds. Although not always beneficial to patients, the procedures they employed involved much care and caution.

In addition to addressing the physical aspects of disease, Greek doctors did not neglect the spiritual side of healing. When their own efforts failed, they recommended that their patients visit one of the many "asclepieia" – temples dedicated to the patron god of physicians, Asclepius, and his daughters, Hygeia (health) and Panacea (healing). At the temples, patients relaxed in beautiful surroundings and read inscriptions on marble pillars that told of miraculous remedies provided by the gods. It was believed that if they spent the night in the sacred hall, Asclepius would appear to them as they slept and give them a "dream drug" or even perform "dream surgery," and cure them.

The greatest of all doctors in ancient Greece was Hippocrates. A physician and surgeon, he headed a medical school on the Aegean island of Kos. His work and that of his followers is contained in the Corpus Hippocraticum, over 70 volumes that range in content from detailed case histories to thoughts on the practice of medicine, the effects of the environment on health and, most importantly, prognosis. It was the Hippocratic school's concentration on the latter that distinguished it from other medical schools of thought that were active at the time. While non-Hippocratic doctors only tried to identify symptoms and make diagnoses, the Kos physicians went one step further and tried to predict a patient's prospects of recovery.

Climate change refers to long-term shifts in global temperatures and weather patterns. While some climate variation is natural, scientists agree that since the mid-twentieth century, human activities have been the dominant cause of the changes observed. The burning of fossil fuels such as coal, oil, and natural gas releases large quantities of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. These gases trap heat from the sun, causing the planet to warm gradually, a process known as the greenhouse effect. The consequences of climate change are already visible: rising sea levels, more frequent and severe weather events, melting glaciers, and disruptions to ecosystems. Some regions face increased flooding, while others experience prolonged droughts. If current trends continue, scientists warn that many coastal cities could be submerged by the end of the century. International efforts to address climate change, most notably the Paris Agreement of 2015, have sought to limit global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, but progress has been slow and uneven.

Camels are famous for living in hot, dry deserts. Many people think that a camel keeps water in its hump, but this is not true. The hump is full of fat, which the camel uses for energy when there is no food. A camel can drink a huge amount of water very quickly — more than 100 liters in about ten minutes — and then walk for days without drinking again. Camels also have long eyelashes that protect their eyes from sand, and wide feet that help them walk on soft ground. For thousands of years, people in the desert have used camels to carry heavy loads across long distances.

Antibiotics are medicines that kill or inhibit the growth of bacteria, and they have saved countless lives since their introduction in the twentieth century. The first antibiotic, penicillin, was discovered accidentally by Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming in 1928, when he noticed that mold growing on a petri dish was killing the bacteria around it. The development of penicillin and subsequent antibiotics transformed medicine, making previously deadly infections treatable and enabling complex surgical procedures to be carried out with greatly reduced risk of infection. However, the overuse and misuse of antibiotics has led to a serious global health problem: antibiotic resistance. When bacteria are exposed to antibiotics repeatedly, they can evolve to survive the treatment, creating strains of bacteria that are extremely difficult or impossible to treat. This process is accelerated when patients do not complete their full course of antibiotics or when the drugs are used unnecessarily for viral infections, against which they have no effect. The World Health Organization has identified antibiotic resistance as one of the greatest threats to global health.

The Internet, which began as a small military communications network in the United States in the late 1960s, has grown into the largest communications network in history, connecting billions of people and devices around the world. The original network, called ARPANET, was designed to allow military computers to share information even if parts of the network were destroyed in a nuclear attack. The key innovation was a system called "packet switching," which broke data into small pieces that could travel by different routes and be reassembled at their destination.

The Internet became available to the general public in the early 1990s, following the invention of the World Wide Web by British scientist Tim Berners-Lee. The Web made it simple for users without technical expertise to navigate the Internet by clicking on links. By the end of the 1990s, the number of Internet users had grown from a few million to hundreds of millions. Today, more than five billion people use the Internet.

The Internet has transformed nearly every aspect of modern life, from commerce and education to entertainment and social interaction. However, it has also created new challenges. The spread of misinformation has become a serious problem, as false news stories can reach millions of people within minutes. Privacy concerns have grown as companies and governments collect vast amounts of personal data. Cybercrime has emerged as a major threat, costing the global economy trillions of dollars each year.

On July 20, 1969, American astronaut Neil Armstrong became the first human to walk on the Moon. The mission, known as Apollo 11, was the culmination of nearly a decade of intensive effort by NASA. Armstrong and fellow astronaut Buzz Aldrin spent about two and a half hours exploring the lunar surface, while Michael Collins orbited above in the command module. Armstrong famously described the moment as one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind. The Apollo program had been launched in direct response to the Soviet Union's early lead in the Space Race, which had alarmed the American public following the launch of Sputnik in 1957. The Moon landing demonstrated the power of human determination and scientific innovation, as well as the geopolitical rivalry that drove nations to extraordinary achievements. Since Apollo 11, only eleven more astronauts have walked on the Moon, all between 1969 and 1972.

Bees are small insects, but they do a very big job. When a bee visits a flower, it drinks a sweet liquid called nectar. At the same time, yellow dust called pollen sticks to its body. When the bee flies to the next flower, some of the pollen falls off. This helps the flowers make seeds and fruit. Without bees, many plants could not grow. Bees also use the nectar to make honey, which they store in their home, the hive. People have kept bees for thousands of years and collect honey from the hives.

The first bicycles, built in the early 1800s, looked very different from the ones we ride today. They had no pedals, so riders pushed themselves along the ground with their feet. Pedals were added around 1860, and for a while bicycles had one huge front wheel and one tiny back wheel. These tall machines were fast but dangerous, and riders often fell. In the 1880s, the safety bicycle appeared, with two wheels of equal size and a chain connecting the pedals to the back wheel. It was cheaper, safer, and easier to ride than earlier models. Millions of people bought it, and cycling quickly became a popular way to travel.

A green roof is a layer of plants growing on top of a building. Although the idea seems modern, people have covered roofs with grass for centuries in cold climates, where the plants helped keep houses warm. Today, cities encourage green roofs for different reasons. The plants absorb rainwater, which reduces flooding after heavy storms. They also cool the building beneath them, lowering the need for air conditioning in summer. In addition, green roofs provide space for birds and insects that struggle to survive in crowded urban areas. Critics point out that green roofs are expensive to install and maintain. Supporters respond that the long-term savings in energy, together with the environmental benefits, outweigh the initial costs.

In medical research, patients sometimes improve after receiving a treatment that contains no active ingredient at all. This puzzling phenomenon, known as the placebo effect, has been documented for centuries, yet its mechanisms are still not fully understood. Expectation appears to play a central role: when patients believe a treatment will help them, their brains may release chemicals that genuinely relieve pain or reduce stress. The effect is so powerful that new drugs must outperform a placebo in controlled trials before they are approved for use. Some researchers argue that doctors should harness the placebo effect deliberately, since it can produce real benefits at little cost. Others warn that doing so involves deceiving patients, a practice that could undermine the trust on which medicine depends.

In 1901, divers exploring an ancient shipwreck near the Greek island of Antikythera recovered a lump of corroded bronze that would ultimately transform our understanding of ancient technology. Decades of painstaking analysis revealed the fragments to be the remains of an intricate geared device, now dated to the second century BCE, capable of predicting eclipses and modeling the movements of the sun and moon with astonishing precision. Nothing of comparable sophistication appears in the archaeological record for well over a thousand years afterward, a gap that has fueled speculation about how much ancient knowledge has simply vanished. Scholars caution, however, against inferring that such devices were common: the mechanism may have been an exceptional commission for a wealthy patron rather than a representative product of its age. What is beyond dispute is that its discovery forced historians to abandon the comfortable assumption that mechanical complexity is an exclusively modern achievement.

Of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken today, linguists estimate that nearly half may disappear by the end of the century. A language dies when its last fluent speakers pass away without transmitting it to the next generation — a process usually driven not by choice but by economic and social pressure, as parents conclude that a dominant national language offers their children better prospects. The loss is more than sentimental. Each language encodes distinctive knowledge: names for local plants and their medicinal uses, oral histories, and ways of describing the world that have no exact equivalent elsewhere. When a language vanishes, this accumulated knowledge frequently vanishes with it. Revival is difficult but not impossible. Hebrew was transformed from a largely liturgical language into the mother tongue of millions, and Welsh and Maori have regained ground through immersion schools and broadcasting. Such successes, researchers note, share one condition: communities that treat the language not as a museum piece but as a living tool for daily life.

In 2015, a consortium of researchers undertook to replicate one hundred prominent psychology experiments and succeeded in fewer than forty cases — a result that sent tremors through the discipline and lent its name to what is now called the replication crisis. The causes are less scandalous than structural. Journals have long favored novel, striking findings over careful confirmations, giving researchers little incentive to verify published work. Small sample sizes and flexible analytic choices allow chance results to masquerade as discoveries. Critics who declare the science broken, however, may be drawing the wrong lesson. Failed replication does not necessarily expose fraud or incompetence; subtle differences in populations, procedures, and eras can legitimately produce divergent outcomes. Indeed, some argue the crisis is better described as a correction — evidence that science's machinery of self-scrutiny, however slow, ultimately functions. The reforms it has produced, including preregistration of hypotheses and the routine sharing of data, may prove more valuable than the disturbing headline that started it all.

Housed in a Yale library vault lies a small vellum codex that has humbled generations of scholars: the Voynich manuscript, named for the book dealer who acquired it in 1912. Its pages combine botanical illustrations of plants that match no known species, astrological diagrams, and roughly 240 pages of flowing script in an alphabet found nowhere else. Radiocarbon dating places the vellum in the early fifteenth century, ruling out suspicions that Voynich himself had forged it. Cryptographers who cracked wartime ciphers, among them the celebrated William Friedman, spent decades on the text and retired defeated. Statistical analyses deepen the enigma: the script obeys word-frequency patterns characteristic of natural languages, which argues against random gibberish, yet it resists every method that unlocks known ciphers. Three rival camps persist — an unknown natural language, an uncracked cipher, or an elaborate medieval hoax designed to fleece a wealthy collector. Each theory accounts for some evidence while stumbling over the rest, and periodic announcements of a solution have so far collapsed under scrutiny.

vocabulary.definition: To combine parts into a whole; to bring together.
vocabulary.example_sentence: The curriculum integrates science and mathematics.

vocabulary.definition: Living or occurring at the same time; belonging to the present time
vocabulary.example_sentence: The museum focused on contemporary art from the past decade.
